Incidents 03 Apr 2023 minute read Georgy Kucherin Vasily Berdnikov Vilen Kamalov Authors Georgy Kucherin Vasily Berdnikov Vilen Kamalov On March 29, Crowdstrike published a report about a supply chain attack conducted via 3CXDesktopApp, a popular VoIP program. Since then, the security community has started analyzing the attack and sharing their findings. The following has been discovered so far: The infection is spread via 3CXDesktopApp MSI installers. An installer for macOS has also been trojanized. The malicious installation package contains an infected dll library that decrypts a shellcode from the d3dcompiler_47.dll library’s overlay and executes it. The decrypted payload extracts C2 server URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository (the repository is removed). The payload connects to one of the C2 servers, downloads an infostealer and starts it. The infostealer collects system information and browser history, then sends it to the C2 server. As we reviewed available reports on the 3CX attack, we began wondering if the compromise concluded with the infostealer or further implants followed. To answer that question, we decided to review the telemetry we had on the campaign. On one of the machines, we observed a DLL named guard64.dll, which was loaded into the infected 3CXDesktopApp.exe process. Interestingly enough, we opened an investigation into a case linked to that DLL on March 21, about a week before the supply chain attack was discovered. A DLL with that name was used in recent deployments of a backdoor that we dubbed “Gopuram” and had been tracking internally since 2020. Three years ago, we were investigating an infection of a cryptocurrency company located in Southeast Asia. During the investigation, we found that Gopuram coexisted on victim machines with AppleJeus , a backdoor attributed to the Korean-speaking threat actor Lazarus . Over the years, we observed few victims compromised with Gopuram, but the number of infections began to increase in March 2023. As it turned out, the increase was directly related to the 3CX supply chain attack. We found out that the threat actor specifically targeted cryptocurrency companies, dropping the following files on infected machines: C:\\Windows\\system32\\wlbsctrl.dll, a malicious library (MD5: 9f85a07d4b4abff82ca18d990f062a84); C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\TxR\\<machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms, an encrypted shellcode payload. Once dropped, wlbsctrl.dll becomes loaded on every startup by the IKEEXT service via DLL hijacking . We further saw DLLs with the names ualapi.dll and ncobjapi.dll being sideloaded into spoolsv.exe and svchost.exe, respectively. The wlbsctrl.dll library is responsible for decrypting and executing the shellcode stored in the C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\TxR directory. The decryption is notably performed through the CryptUnprotectData API function that uses a different encryption key internally on every machine. This makes it difficult for researchers to decrypt the payload from the file without physical access to the victim machines. Snippet of the loading function using CryptUnprotectData The component loaded by the library is Gopuram’s main module. As mentioned above, its name in the export directory is guard64.dll. The job of the main module is to connect to a C2 server and request commands. The backdoor implements commands that allow the attackers to interact with the victim’s file system and create processes on the infected machine. Gopuram was additionally observed to launch in-memory modules. Just like the implants used in the 3CX campaign, Gopuram’s modules are DLL files that include an export function named DllGetClassObject. We have observed nine modules so far: Module name Description Ping Pings a host specified in the argument. Connect Connects to a given host via a socket and waits for the server to send data. Registry Manipulates registry (lists, adds, deletes and exports keys). Service Manipulates (creates, lists, starts, stops and deletes) services. Timestomp Performs timestomping on files. Inject Performs payload injections through syscalls via mapping a shellcode to a remote process and creating a remote thread. KDU Kernel Driver Utility that allows an attacker to bypass driver signature enforcement. The utility is used to load an unsigned driver (MD5: F684E10FF1FFCDD32C62E73A11382896). The driver collects information about installed AV filters and writes it to the C:\\Windows\\System32\\catroot2\\edb.chk.log file. Update Encrypts a provided payload and writes it to the C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\TxR\\<machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms file. Net Partially implements features of the net command: management of users, groups, sessions and network shares. The discovery of the new Gopuram infections allowed us to attribute the 3CX campaign to the Lazarus threat actor with medium to high confidence. Our attribution is based on the following facts: While investigating an attack on a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency company in 2020, we found Gopuram coexisting on the same machine with the AppleJeus backdoor, which is attributed to Lazarus. The Gopuram backdoor has been observed in attacks on cryptocurrency companies, which is aligned with the interests of the Lazarus threat actor. While looking for additional implants that used the same loader shellcode as the 3CX implants, we discovered a sample on a multiscanner service (MD5: 933508a9832da1150fcfdbc1ca9bc84c ) loading a payload that uses the wirexpro[.]com C2 server. The same server is listed as an IoC for an AppleJeus campaign by Malwarebytes. First bytes of the loader shellcode used in 3CX and AppleJeus Note, though, that the shellcode is based on open-source code that has been used by other threat actors, for example, SilentBreak. Still, the use of that shellcode along with the 0xF558F4DA constant (which is the ROR13 hash for the string DllGetClassObject) is a more unique pattern. While investigating a malicious MSI file (MD5: ec3f99dd7d9dbce8d704d407b086e84f ) that has been uploaded to a multiscanner service, we observed the following two events: The dll library dropped from the MSI was observed to launch an in-memory payload that contacts the oilycargo[.]com domain. This domain name has previously been attributed to Lazarus by multiple researchers. In our telemetry, we observed AvBugReport.exe, the executable hosting dll, to contain Gopuram’s main module payload, guard64.dll. These four facts allow us to conclude that Lazarus is likely the threat actor deploying the Gopuram backdoor. As for the victims in our telemetry, installations of the infected 3CX software are located all over the world, with the highest infection figures observed in Brazil, Germany, Italy and France. As the Gopuram backdoor has been deployed to less than ten infected machines, it indicates that attackers used Gopuram with surgical precision. We additionally observed that the attackers have a specific interest in cryptocurrency companies. As it turns out, the infostealer is not the only malicious payload deployed during the 3CX supply chain attack. The threat actor behind Gopuram additionally infects target machines with the full-fledged modular Gopuram backdoor. We believe that Gopuram is the main implant and the final payload in the attack chain. Our investigation of the 3CX campaign is still far from complete. We will continue analyzing the deployed implants to find out more details about the toolset used in the supply chain attack. arguments.source_title: Mandiant 3CX Software Supply Chain Compromise investigation
arguments.text: Mandiant reports the initial 3CX network compromise vector was malicious software downloaded from Trading Technologies' website: a tampered X_TRADER installer, an earlier software supply-chain compromise. The attacker used X_TRADER on a 3CX employee machine, then moved laterally in 3CX, harvested credentials, and compromised both Windows and macOS build environments. Windows build environment: TAXHAUL launcher and COLDCAT downloader persisted via IKEEXT DLL search-order hijacking with LocalSystem privileges. macOS build server: POOLRAT backdoor persisted with Launch Daemons; prior reporting called it SIMPLESEA, but Mandiant identified it as POOLRAT. The attacker then trojanized 3CX DesktopApp builds. Affected 3CX DesktopApp 18.12.416 and earlier ran SUDDENICON, which obtained C2 URLs from encrypted GitHub-hosted icons and downloaded ICONICSTEALER browser-information dataminer. Mandiant tracks the activity as UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assesses with moderate confidence UNC4736 is related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity; evidence includes overlap with Trading Technologies compromise and POOLRAT associated with CoinGoTrade/JMT Trading AppleJeus activity. Mandiant notes weak infrastructure overlap with suspected APT43 clusters UNC3782 and UNC4469. The X_TRADER and 3CX samples shared RC4 key, SIGFLIP, DAVESHELL, hardcoded cookie variable, and AES-256-GCM encryption. Mandiant says this was a cascading supply-chain compromise.

# CASE BACKGROUND

This investigation concerns the 2023 compromise of the 3CX DesktopApp through a software supply-chain attack. The supplied evidence describes two linked compromises:

1. A tampered X_TRADER installer from Trading Technologies’ website infected a 3CX employee’s machine.
2. The attackers used that access to move laterally into 3CX development infrastructure and distribute trojanized 3CX DesktopApp installers to customers. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

The campaign affected Windows and macOS versions of the 3CX DesktopApp. Reported affected versions included Windows 18.12.407 and 18.12.416, and macOS 18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416. [SRC-009]

# GENERAL OBJECTIVES

- Reconstruct the intrusion and software-supply-chain compromise chain.
- Identify the malware and persistence mechanisms used on Windows and macOS.
- Describe the trojanized 3CX DesktopApp payloads and their capabilities.
- Distinguish Mandiant’s UNC4736 cluster assessment from Lazarus attribution in other reporting.
- Identify the strength and limitations of the available attribution evidence.
- Preserve the distinction between established technical facts and analytical assessments.

# LEGAL ISSUES

The conduct described may implicate:

- Unauthorized access to employee systems and development infrastructure.
- Credential theft and unauthorized use of harvested credentials.
- Malware deployment and persistence.
- Tampering with software-build environments.
- Distribution of malicious software to downstream customers.
- Unauthorized collection of system information, browser data, and stored credentials.
- Potential targeting of cryptocurrency-related organizations.

The evidence supplied supports describing these as investigative issues, but it does not identify specific defendants, jurisdictions, criminal charges, or applicable statutes. Legal conclusions about liability or attribution should therefore not be drawn solely from this report.

# INVESTIGATION PREPARATION

The investigation was limited to the nine benchmark sources identified as SRC-001 through SRC-009. No additional internet material was used.

The supplied context does not include the underlying source URLs. Accordingly, the references below preserve the benchmark source identifiers, but cannot provide the required direct URLs without risking fabrication. The source identifiers should be mapped to their original URLs before operational, legal, or evidentiary use.

The following distinctions were applied:

- Technical observations are treated separately from attribution assessments.
- Mandiant’s designation **UNC4736** is not equated with the generic **Lazarus Group** label.
- “North Korean nexus,” “Lazarus,” and “AppleJeus-related” are reported as source-specific assessments rather than established identities.
- Confidence levels and stated uncertainties are retained.

# OSINT STEPS

1. **Established the initial compromise vector.**  
   The initial access came from a malicious X_TRADER installer downloaded from Trading Technologies’ website. The installer was itself associated with an earlier software supply-chain compromise. [SRC-003]

2. **Reconstructed lateral movement and development compromise.**  
   X_TRADER infected a 3CX employee machine, enabled lateral movement, facilitated credential harvesting, and led to compromise of Windows and macOS build environments. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

3. **Identified operating-system-specific malware.**  
   Windows systems received TAXHAUL and COLDCAT. macOS systems received POOLRAT, previously reported as SIMPLESEA. [SRC-003]

4. **Documented persistence mechanisms.**  
   COLDCAT persisted through IKEEXT DLL search-order hijacking with LocalSystem privileges. POOLRAT persisted through Launch Daemons on macOS. [SRC-003]

5. **Reconstructed the downstream supply-chain attack.**  
   Attackers trojanized 3CX DesktopApp builds, causing customers to receive infected Windows and macOS packages. [SRC-003] [SRC-008] [SRC-009]

6. **Characterized the final-stage payload chain.**  
   SUDDENICON extracted command-and-control URLs from encrypted icon files hosted on GitHub and downloaded ICONICSTEALER. Other reporting identified Gopuram as a final-stage backdoor. [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-009]

7. **Compared attribution assessments.**  
   Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736 and assessed, with moderate confidence, a relationship to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky attributed the operation to Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence, while other reporting described North Korean attribution but retained uncertainty about the campaign’s full objectives. [SRC-002] [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-007]

8. **Compared technical similarities between the X_TRADER and 3CX compromises.**  
   Mandiant identified shared technical characteristics including the same RC4 key, SIGFLIP, DAVESHELL, a hardcoded cookie variable, and AES-256-GCM encryption. [SRC-003]

# FINDINGS

## 1. What was the initial compromise vector?

The initial compromise was a malicious X_TRADER installer downloaded from Trading Technologies’ website. The X_TRADER installer was described as originating from an earlier software supply-chain compromise and infected a 3CX employee machine. [SRC-003]

## 2. How did the attackers progress from the employee compromise to the 3CX supply-chain compromise?

The attackers used X_TRADER-enabled access to move laterally through 3CX, harvest credentials, and compromise both Windows and macOS build environments. They then corrupted the 3CX DesktopApp build process or resulting installers, distributing infected software to customers. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

## 3. What malware and persistence mechanisms were used?

On Windows, TAXHAUL and COLDCAT were deployed. COLDCAT persisted through IKEEXT DLL search-order hijacking and operated with LocalSystem privileges. On macOS, POOLRAT persisted through Launch Daemons; earlier reporting referred to the malware as SIMPLESEA, but Mandiant identified it as POOLRAT. [SRC-003]

## 4. What did the trojanized 3CX DesktopApp do?

Affected 3CX DesktopApp versions executed SUDDENICON. SUDDENICON retrieved command-and-control URLs from encrypted icon files hosted on GitHub and downloaded ICONICSTEALER, a browser-information dataminer. The malicious application could collect system information and steal data or stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles. [SRC-003] [SRC-009]

## 5. Which 3CX versions were reported as affected?

The supplied Singapore Cyber Security Agency reporting identified Windows versions 18.12.407 and 18.12.416, and macOS versions 18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416. Mandiant additionally described 3CX DesktopApp version 18.12.416 and earlier as affected by SUDDENICON. [SRC-003] [SRC-009]

## 6. What is the attribution assessment?

Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster, and assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Mandiant also noted weak infrastructure overlap with suspected APT43 clusters UNC3782 and UNC4469. [SRC-003]

Kaspersky attributed the campaign to Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence, based on the coexistence of Gopuram with AppleJeus, cryptocurrency targeting, shared loader shellcode and infrastructure, and domains previously attributed to Lazarus. [SRC-004]

These are not identical attribution statements. **UNC4736 is Mandiant’s cluster label and assessment; Lazarus is Kaspersky’s attribution and a broader label used in public reporting.** SRC-007 cautions that Lazarus is an umbrella term and that individual operations may be difficult to attribute with high confidence. [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-007]

## 7. What was the apparent targeting and operational objective?

Gopuram was observed on fewer than ten machines and was associated with targeting cryptocurrency firms. The evidence indicates credential theft, browser-data theft, system-information collection, and access to cryptocurrency-related organizations. However, SRC-002 records uncertainty regarding the campaign’s full objectives, so the complete operational purpose remains unresolved. [SRC-002] [SRC-009]

# CONCLUSION

The evidence supports a two-stage software-supply-chain compromise. First, a tampered X_TRADER installer from Trading Technologies’ website compromised a 3CX employee and enabled lateral movement into 3CX’s development environment. Second, the attackers compromised 3CX build infrastructure and distributed trojanized DesktopApp packages to customers. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

The technical chain is well documented: X_TRADER access, credential harvesting, compromise of Windows and macOS build environments, deployment of TAXHAUL, COLDCAT, and POOLRAT, trojanization of 3CX builds, execution of SUDDENICON, retrieval of GitHub-hosted command-and-control URLs, and deployment of ICONICSTEALER or Gopuram-related payloads. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

Attribution must remain qualified. Mandiant’s assessment concerns **UNC4736** and its suspected relationship to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky separately assessed **Lazarus** attribution with medium-to-high confidence. SRC-007 warns that Lazarus is often used as an umbrella term and that operation-level attribution can be difficult. The supplied evidence therefore supports a probable North Korean nexus, but does not justify treating UNC4736 and Lazarus as interchangeable identities or presenting attribution as conclusively established. [SRC-002] [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-007]

# REFERENCES

> The case context supplied source identifiers but did not supply the underlying URLs. Direct URLs are therefore unavailable in this report and should be added from the benchmark’s source registry before formal citation.

- **SRC-001** — Benchmark source; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-002** — Reporting on North Korean attribution, Smooth Operator, Gopuram, and campaign uncertainty; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-003** — Mandiant/Google Cloud reporting on UNC4736, X_TRADER, the 3CX compromise, malware, and technical similarities; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-004** — Reporting on the trojanized 3CX packages, Gopuram, and Lazarus attribution; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-005** — Benchmark source; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-006** — Benchmark source; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-007** — Reporting identifying Lazarus as a North Korean state-sponsored group and discussing attribution limitations; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-008** — Reporting describing the two linked supply-chain attacks; URL not supplied in case context.
- **SRC-009** — Singapore Cyber Security Agency advisory dated 31 March 2023 concerning affected 3CX versions and capabilities; URL not supplied in case context.

## 2. How did the attackers progress from the employee compromise to the 3CX supply-chain compromise?

The attackers used X_TRADER-enabled access to move laterally through 3CX, harvest credentials, and compromise both Windows and macOS build environments. They then corrupted the 3CX DesktopApp build process or resulting installers, distributing infected software to customers. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

## 3. What malware and persistence mechanisms were used?

On Windows, TAXHAUL and COLDCAT were deployed. COLDCAT persisted through IKEEXT DLL search-order hijacking and operated with LocalSystem privileges. On macOS, POOLRAT persisted through Launch Daemons; earlier reporting referred to the malware as SIMPLESEA, but Mandiant identified it as POOLRAT. [SRC-003]

## 4. What did the trojanized 3CX DesktopApp do?

Affected 3CX DesktopApp versions executed SUDDENICON. SUDDENICON retrieved command-and-control URLs from encrypted icon files hosted on GitHub and downloaded ICONICSTEALER, a browser-information dataminer. The malicious application could collect system information and steal data or stored credentials from Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Firefox profiles. [SRC-003] [SRC-009]

## 5. Which 3CX versions were reported as affected?

The supplied Singapore Cyber Security Agency reporting identified Windows versions 18.12.407 and 18.12.416, and macOS versions 18.11.1213, 18.12.402, 18.12.407, and 18.12.416. Mandiant additionally described 3CX DesktopApp version 18.12.416 and earlier as affected by SUDDENICON. [SRC-003] [SRC-009]

## 6. What is the attribution assessment?

Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster, and assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Mandiant also noted weak infrastructure overlap with suspected APT43 clusters UNC3782 and UNC4469. [SRC-003]

Kaspersky attributed the campaign to Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence, based on the coexistence of Gopuram with AppleJeus, cryptocurrency targeting, shared loader shellcode and infrastructure, and domains previously attributed to Lazarus. [SRC-004]

These are not identical attribution statements. **UNC4736 is Mandiant’s cluster label and assessment; Lazarus is Kaspersky’s attribution and a broader label used in public reporting.** SRC-007 cautions that Lazarus is an umbrella term and that individual operations may be difficult to attribute with high confidence. [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-007]

## 7. What was the apparent targeting and operational objective?

Gopuram was observed on fewer than ten machines and was associated with targeting cryptocurrency firms. The evidence indicates credential theft, browser-data theft, system-information collection, and access to cryptocurrency-related organizations. However, SRC-002 records uncertainty regarding the campaign’s full objectives, so the complete operational purpose remains unresolved. [SRC-002] [SRC-009]

# CONCLUSION

The evidence supports a two-stage software-supply-chain compromise. First, a tampered X_TRADER installer from Trading Technologies’ website compromised a 3CX employee and enabled lateral movement into 3CX’s development environment. Second, the attackers compromised 3CX build infrastructure and distributed trojanized DesktopApp packages to customers. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

The technical chain is well documented: X_TRADER access, credential harvesting, compromise of Windows and macOS build environments, deployment of TAXHAUL, COLDCAT, and POOLRAT, trojanization of 3CX builds, execution of SUDDENICON, retrieval of GitHub-hosted command-and-control URLs, and deployment of ICONICSTEALER or Gopuram-related payloads. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

Attribution must remain qualified. Mandiant’s assessment concerns **UNC4736** and its suspected relationship to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky separately assessed **Lazarus** attribution with medium-to-high confidence. SRC-007 warns that Lazarus is often used as an umbrella term and that operation-level attribution can be difficult. The supplied evidence therefore supports a probable North Korean nexus, but does not justify treating UNC4736 and Lazarus as interchangeable identities or presenting attribution as conclusively established. [SRC-002] [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-007]
